title: Overseas Study Report - Medical University of Gdansk / Medical University of Vienna
paragraphs: I had the opportunity to do clerkships abroad at the Medical University of Gdansk in Poland and the Medical University of Vienna in Austria through the Nagoya University exchange program. It was my first overseas trip and I was somewhat anxious at first, but every day was fresh and stimulating, and I think I gained truly valuable experience. My schedule was three weeks of neurosurgery in Gdansk, and in Vienna four weeks of emergency and critical care medicine and four weeks of neurosurgery.

Poland is a former socialist country that has now converted to capitalism and is in the midst of economic growth. The hospital where I did my clerkship had been rebuilt only last year and was very clean, with all the latest equipment. I could not understand the rounds and conferences in Polish, but in surgery I was actively allowed to serve as an assistant and was even entrusted with skin suturing, so although it was short, it was a fulfilling clerkship. Because of historical reasons and a similarity in national character, Polish people are very pro-Japanese, and Professor Wozniak of the Department of Biochemistry, who served as my coordinator, also loved Japan very much and treated me very well. The old town, where traces of the former socialist era remain, was very beautiful, prices were low and the food was delicious, and I regretted that three weeks was such a short stay.

Vienna, famous as the city of music, is a city similar in population and area to Nagoya and is very famous as a tourist destination, but the Medical University of Vienna, where I did my clerkship, is a giant hospital with 2245 beds, second in the world and first in Europe, and it is famous for its concentrated advanced medicine and the various transport systems that cover its huge size.

The Department of Emergency Medicine is divided into emergency internal medicine, Notfall, and trauma surgery, Unfall, and Notfall handles emergency care other than trauma. It also has a helipad, and severely ill patients are brought in one after another even from outside the city of Vienna. It is the same as in Japan in that it becomes busy from the evening, after the regular outpatient clinics close, but a major difference from Japan is that a doctor also rides in the ambulance, so a rough diagnosis has been made by the time the patient is transported to the university hospital. This makes it possible to give the hospital more detailed information and instructions, and I was moved by the efficiency with which everything necessary for treatment was ready by the time the patient arrived.

The Department of Neurosurgery of the Medical University of Vienna is in a separate building. It is a neurosurgery department leading the world under Professor Knosp, who created the "Knosp classification" of pituitary tumors using MRI, and besides me, doctors who had already obtained specialist qualifications from Taiwan, Ukraine and elsewhere were there as exchange students. The Vienna neurosurgery department, the origin from which Nagoya University neurosurgery was imported, has three operating rooms, one operating room for DBS and one angiography room, and was a very active neurosurgery department.

The clerkship in Vienna as a whole tested my proactiveness greatly. Unlike ERASMS, no special program was prepared for exchange students from Nagoya University, and I was told that the content of the clerkship was "It's all up to you." I joined conferences and rounds, but I could not understand the German even when I listened, and at first I was at a loss. If I wanted to learn, I had no choice but to act on my own. I kept asking questions, and at first I was often shunned and nearly gave up, but as I kept asking without being discouraged, they recognized that I was motivated, and the doctors gradually became friendlier. The fact that I was learning German between clerkship hours also seemed to make a good impression on them. In neurosurgery, after finishing my duty of drawing blood and placing IV lines during rounds every morning, I went to the operating room every day. Every day I observed all the operations to the end, helped with odd jobs, and always asked the operating surgeon questions afterward. Such efforts were recognized, and one day Associate Professor Bavinzski (the number one in the cerebrovascular division of Vienna neurosurgery) spoke to me, and for the last ten days I was allowed to be first assistant every day, directly guided in Associate Professor Bavinzski's operations. It was my first time assisting under a microscope. He taught me the details of the surgery in a very easy-to-understand way, and in the end he even invited me to a seminar for improving cerebrovascular surgery techniques, where neurosurgeons gather from all over Europe. I was deeply impressed by Associate Professor Bavinzski's words: "A surgeon is like a conductor in music. Everything has a reason, even the slightest movement. An orchestra conductor gives very detailed instructions to every instrument, but the accumulation of those fine controls creates a single piece. Watching an operation vaguely is no study. Watch and learn every detail of the technique."

Through this experience, first, I learned the joy of widening one's world through communication in a foreign language. With English alone I made a great many friends during my time abroad and fully enjoyed intercultural communication. Second, if you have a clear goal, make every effort you can and keep a proactive attitude, results will surely follow. Chances are proportional to motivation. I want to continue to value the proactiveness I cultivated in this experience.

Finally, I would like to take this opportunity to express my sincere gratitude to Dr. 粕屋 and the staff of the International Exchange Office and the academic affairs office who gave me such a valuable opportunity, to Professor 若林 of neurosurgery who introduced me to Professor Knosp, to the seniors who gave me a lot of advice, and to all my classmates who studied together with me. Thank you very much.
